name: diet
title: The Ray Peat diet
question: What was the diet Peat recommended?
description: What Ray Peat advocated about diet: milk, cheese, fruit and shellfish, few polyunsaturated fats, less starch, and protein with more gelatin.
intro: According to Peat, the healthiest diet is based on plenty of protein, few unsaturated fats, little iron and lots of antioxidants, with low or moderate starch intake [1]. In practice, for him this means relying on milk, cheese, eggs, shellfish, fruit and coconut oil [1]. He also held that polyunsaturated vegetable oils are one of the big problems of modern eating [2].

sections.heading: The foods at the core of his diet
paragraphs: Peat proposed that a large part of the diet be milk, cheese, eggs, shellfish, fruit and coconut oil, with vitamin E and salt as the safest supplements [1]. He considered that this pattern served as an anti-ageing diet and also to prevent and treat diabetes and connective tissue diseases [1].

He warned that amino acids, especially those in eggs, stimulate insulin secretion. According to him, this can cause hypoglycaemia and, with it, the release of cortisol [1]. He thought that having fruit or another carbohydrate, coconut oil and salt in the same meal reduces that effect of protein [1].

sections.heading: Milk and cheese for weight loss
paragraphs: To lose weight, Peat described first a period without eating and then a diet of low-fat milk and cheese, with some orange juice and occasionally eggs and oysters [3]. He held that milk and cheese as the base greatly increase heat production, energy metabolism and oxygen consumption, which makes losing weight easier [3].

In his opinion, calcium and vitamin D support thyroid hormone, and their deficiency is very common and slows metabolism [3]. He added that a high intake of polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA) impairs both vitamin D metabolism and that of the thyroid [3]. He also wanted to lower dietary phosphorus relative to calcium [3].

sections.heading: Fats: why he avoided seed oils
paragraphs: Peat summed up that unsaturated fats cause ageing, clotting, inflammation, cancer and weight gain, and recommended avoiding corn, soy, safflower, flax, cottonseed, rapeseed, peanut and sesame oils [2]. He told how the seed oil industry lost its market in paints and varnishes and how its crops went to fattening animals and then to being promoted for people [2]. According to him, the talk about cholesterol was just a marketing tool of that industry [2].

In his list of practical guidelines, he advised using coconut oil, butter and olive oil, as well as vitamin E [2]. He said that lard is usually as toxic as those oils, because pigs are fed corn and soy, and that lean meat is better [2]. He considered dried fish and shellfish once or twice a week good, and advised against cod liver oil [2]. He also stated that unsaturated fats intensify the harmful effects of estrogens [2].

sections.heading: Sugar and fruit versus starch
paragraphs: Peat gave great importance to a 1938 experiment in which a man lived for six months on sucrose syrup, milk, cottage cheese and orange juice [4]. The researchers observed that his usual tiredness disappeared, that his high blood pressure and high cholesterol returned to normal and that his lifelong migraines stopped [4][5]. For Peat, the most interesting thing was that his blood phosphate fell [4].

He interpreted those results as a sign that polyunsaturated fats lower metabolism and hinder the use of sugars, so the normal diet would be diabetogenic [5]. Even so, he believed sugars are healthier in the long run when they come with minerals, as in milk and fruit [6]. He preferred fruit to grains because, calorie for calorie, starch is more fattening than sucrose and also feeds gut bacteria [7].

sections.heading: Grains, legumes and starches
paragraphs: Peat recommended avoiding grain and legume starches, and using fruit as a main part of the diet to minimise the effects of polyunsaturated fats [6]. He linked coeliac disease and gluten sensitivity with diabetes and hypothyroidism, and added that gluten cross-reacts with an enzyme expressed under the influence of estrogens [6]. According to him, the complex starches of unsprouted or unfermented legumes and grains are hard to digest and can cause gas and intestinal inflammation [7].

He also cited the work of an immunologist according to which large starch granules can pass into the blood, block capillaries and expose the immune system to antigens [8]. If starch is eaten, he suggested cooking it very well, for 40 to 60 minutes, and eating it with fat, which slows its absorption and lets the enzymes soften it [8].

sections.heading: Protein, gelatin and plant toxins
paragraphs: Peat cited a National Academy of Sciences study for the army indicating that even adults with office jobs need at least 100 grams of protein a day [9]. He pointed out that the highest-quality proteins are rich in methionine, cysteine and tryptophan, which can be toxic in excess and cause convulsions or inflammation [9]. That is why he preferred gelatin, which lacks those amino acids, and considered that milk provides anti-stress factors, above all its calcium [9].

He thought that a lack of protein lowers body temperature, slows the thyroid and promotes inflammation and clotting [10]. On plants, he held that seeds contain toxins and that their protein has little value, while fruits, roots and tubers provide many nutrients with few antimetabolic substances [11]. For him, studies on protein requirements were done for the agricultural industry and aimed at the fastest, cheapest growth [12].

faq.q: What foods did Ray Peat recommend?
faq.a: According to Peat, a good part of the diet should be milk, cheese, eggs, shellfish, fruit and coconut oil [1]. He also valued orange juice, and gelatin as a source of protein [3][9].

faq.q: Why did Ray Peat reject polyunsaturated vegetable oils?
faq.a: He held that unsaturated fats cause ageing, clotting, inflammation, cancer and weight gain [2]. He also believed they lower metabolism and that a normal diet containing them promotes diabetes [5].

faq.q: What did Peat think of grains and starch?
faq.a: For him, starch amounts to pure glucose and, calorie for calorie, is more fattening than fruit sugar, as well as feeding gut bacteria [7]. He recommended avoiding grains and legumes, and if starch is eaten, cooking it well and eating it with fat [6][8].

faq.q: How much protein did Ray Peat advocate?
faq.a: He cited a National Academy of Sciences study according to which at least 100 grams of protein a day were needed to work efficiently [9]. He added that much of that amount could come from gelatin, which doesn't have the amino acids he considered excitotoxic [12][9].
